To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the network dismantling and decycing problems are tightly connected and that the minimal size of dismantling set in an Erdos-Renyi random network is of order log N.
the optimal dismantling set is a collective phenomenon and that it can be efficiently computed using a Min-Sum algorithm.

1) the dismantling problem is tightly connected with the decycling problem in a large random network with a prescribed (heavy-tailed) degree distributions; 2) we propose a Min-Sum algorithm that efficiently dismantles networks, including heavy tailed ones for which dismantling and decycing are not equivalent problems; 3) we provide additional insights into dismantling problems and conclude that it is an collective problem and that the optimal dismantling sets are not a collection of individually optimal nodes
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of a fundamental problem of network theory and sheds light on the role of degree distribution in the dismantling problem.
the development of efficient and robust network dismantling methods, which are crucial in many real-life applications, including network control, information propagation, and network robustness.
the problem of dismantling a large network, i.e., finding a minimal set of nodes to be removed in order to disconnect the network.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for a large class of networks, dismantling is a collective phenomenon that cannot be reduced to individual nodes.
the network dismantling and decycing problems are equivalent for a large class of networks.
the network dismantling is a hard problem, which is not solvable in polynomial time.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the network dismantling is an intrinsical collective problem and that the dismantling sets are not the collection of individually well performing nodes.
the network dismantling is not a simple task and it is not possible to dismantle a large network by removing a small number of nodes.
dismantling a network is not as easy as one would think.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dismantling a large network requires a global perspective and that local optimization methods are not sufficient to solve the problem.
dismantling random networks can be achieved with a small fraction of vertices, and the Min-Sum algorithm is able to efficiently identify them.
dismantling random graphs is a tractable problem and that the Min-Sum algorithm provides the optimal solution for a large class of graphs.
